symptoms: Ragged holes in whorl leaves (window pane effect), extensive moist yellowish-brown sawdust-like frass inside the plant funnel, severed growing points (dead hearts), and cobs chewed at tip.
prevention: Plant early with the first effective rains to escape peak moth populations.
Intercrop maize with desmodium or beans (Push-Pull technique) to repel moths and attract natural predators.
Scout fields weekly starting 7 days after emergence; inspect 20 plants in 5 separate field locations in a 'W' pattern.
Place handfuls of dry fine sand or wood ash into whorls to physically abrade and suffocate young larvae.
control: Handpick and crush egg masses and caterpillars in smallholder plots.
Apply biopesticides like neem seed kernel extract (NSKE) or Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) early morning or evening when caterpillars feed.

Where threshold exceeds 20% infested whorls, apply approved synthetic insecticides registered in Malawi (e.g. Chlorantraniliprole / Emamectin benzoate) directing the spray specifically into the whorl funnel.
safeHandling: Wear protective gear (gloves, goggles, long sleeves). Spray early in the morning when wind is low. Strictly observe pre-harvest intervals (PHI).

symptoms: Pinholes in young leaves, internal stalk tunneling causing stunted growth, premature lodging (falling over), and drying of central shoot (dead heart).
prevention: Destroy and burn or compost dry crop residues after harvest to kill overwintering diapausing pupae in old stalks.
Practice crop rotation with non-cereal crops such as groundnuts, soya, or cassava.
Encourage predatory ants, earwigs, and parasitic wasps.
control: Drop granular or dust insecticides or wood ash/chilli powder mixtures into the funnel at knee-height.
Cut down and feed heavily infested early plants to livestock to stop generation spread.
safeHandling: Use PPE during application; keep livestock away from treated fields for the duration of the re-entry period.

symptoms: Severe plant stunting, shortened internodes creating a bushy compact rosette appearance, intense leaf yellowing (chlorosis), leaf distortion, and total absence of pods or shriveled empty shells.
prevention: Plant early immediately after the first soaking rain; early dense canopies deter the aphid vector (Aphis craccivora).
Sow certified resistant varieties such as CG7, Chalimbana 2005, or Nsinjiro.
Maintain close plant spacing (double rows on 75cm ridges, 15cm between stations) so soil is quickly shaded by a ground-cover canopy.
control: Rogue out and destroy diseased plants immediately when symptoms first appear in the field.
Spray aphids with soapy water or botanical neem solution if aphid colonies cluster on stems.
safeHandling: Dispose of rogued virus-infected plants away from the field; wash hands and hoes before moving to healthy plants.

symptoms: Pronounced yellow-green mosaic mottling on leaves, severe leaf distortion and leaf curling, stunted plant stems, and reduced tuber root yields by up to 80%.
prevention: Strictly plant certified disease-free stem cuttings from accredited multiplication nurseries.
Use improved resistant varieties like Sauti, Manyokola, Yizaso, or Chitembwere.
Never take stem cuttings from visibly diseased plants, even if one branch looks green.
control: Rogue (uproot) and burn or bury infected cassava plants during the first 3 months of field establishment.
Control whitefly (Bemisia tabaci) populations by intercropping with maize or beans.
safeHandling: Sterilize machetes and knives used for cutting seed stems between bundles using household bleach or flame.

symptoms: Feathery yellowing along secondary leaf veins without distortion; dark brown streaks on green stems; and corky, dry, yellow-brown necrotic rotting inside the storage roots, making them inedible and unmarketable.
prevention: Use certified CBSD-tolerant planting material released by the Department of Agricultural Research Services (DARS).
Do not transport cassava cuttings from lakeshore high-prevalence areas to uninfected upland districts without official quarantine clearance.
Continuous roguing of infected plants.
control: Harvest early (before month 10) in affected zones to reduce root necrosis progression.
Community-wide replanting with clean certified materials.
safeHandling: Comply with domestic plant quarantine regulations to safeguard non-infected agricultural districts.

symptoms: Water-soaked dark lesions on leaves that rapidly turn black and dry; white fluffy fungal growth underneath leaves in damp mornings; dark greasy rot on stems and firm brown rotten patches on fruits.
prevention: Avoid overhead watering; use furrow, bucket-basin, or drip irrigation to keep tomato foliage dry.
Stake vines and prune lower suckers to maintain strong air circulation through the canopy.
Mulch soil around plants to prevent rainwater splash from carrying soil-borne spores onto leaves.
Rotate with non-solanaceous crops (avoid land following potatoes, eggplants, or peppers).
control: Spray protective copper-based fungicides (Copper oxychloride) or Mancozeb before the onset of rain or cool damp misty spells.
Remove and bury infected fruit and leaves immediately. Do not throw into home compost piles.
safeHandling: Always wear rubber gloves, mask, and goggles when mixing and spraying fungicides. Wash knapsack sprayers thoroughly away from drinking wells.

symptoms: Irregular transparent blotch mines inside tomato leaves; caterpillars boring directly into stems, flower buds, and green/ripe fruit creating dark entry holes with black frass.
prevention: Install yellow sticky traps and delta pheromone traps in nurseries and fields for early moth monitoring.
Produce seedlings under insect-proof netting.
Remove and destroy wild nightshade weeds around tomato beds.
control: Handpick and crush mined leaves in early stages.
Rotate chemical classes with different modes of action (e.g. Chlorantraniliprole, Abamectin, Spinosad) to prevent rapid pesticide resistance.
safeHandling: Adhere strictly to labeled pre-harvest intervals (PHI) to avoid toxic pesticide residues on fresh market tomatoes.

symptoms: Severe structural destruction of stored maize and dried cassava. Grain reduced to copious amounts of white flour-like dust within weeks. Holes bored through timber cribs and storage sacks.
prevention: Clean, sweep, and burn old grain dust and residues from nkhokwe, granaries, and store rooms before storing new harvest.
Thoroughly sun-dry grain to below 13.5% moisture.
Store shelled maize in multi-layer airtight hermetic bags (e.g., PICS bags) without chemicals.
Ensure cribs have rodent guards and corrugated iron roofing.
control: Treat clean shelled grain with approved two-component grain protectant dust containing an organophosphate and pyrethroid (e.g., Actellic Gold / Super Guard).
Fumigate commercial bulk silos with phosphine tablets under strict certified extension supervision.
safeHandling: Never consume freshly dusted grain before the specified withholding period (usually 14 to 30 days). Phosphine fumigation requires professional certification.
